lessons.title: Relocate Toward Useful Targets
lessons.question: Can the attacked knight remain active while Black prepares to challenge White's advanced central pawn?
lessons.takeaway: With ...Ng4, Black saves the attacked knight without surrendering its activity. It attacks e5 alongside the c6 knight and also eyes f2. White's advanced pawn therefore remains a responsibility, not just a space advantage. Black has spent another knight move, so development and a central challenge must follow; the knight's threatening appearance does not justify an unsupported raid.
lessons.intent: White has faster kingside development, while Black has an extra central pawn and pressure on e5. The knight keeps contact with useful targets rather than retreating to the back rank. Its exposed placement also gives White a future opportunity to challenge it with a pawn.
lessons.plan: White can castle and bring the rook to e1 to reinforce the center. The supplied continuation has Black develop with ...Be7 and challenge e5 with ...d6. White then exchanges the advanced pawn before recovering d4. Both players should connect development with that central resolution rather than focus exclusively on f2.
lessons.tactic: Both black knights attack e5, while White's f3 knight is its only current defender. That makes moving the defender away a concrete decision, not an automatic recapture on d4. The attack on f2 is a separate resource; nothing supplied here establishes an immediate winning knight sacrifice.
lessons.theme: White's pawn advance has produced an active knight relocation, not a passive retreat. This branch connects the struggle over e5 with the threats Black may later develop against White's king.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...d5 immediately counterattacks the c4 bishop, whereas ...Ng4 saves the knight first and maintains pressure on e5. Both are active responses. Compare the obligations each creates for White and how Black will finish development afterward.

lessons.title: Connect King Safety with Central Support
lessons.question: How can White improve king safety while preparing to reinforce the contested central pawn?
lessons.takeaway: Castling removes the king from the central files and brings the rook within reach of e1. White still needs to resolve the pressure on e5 before recovering d4, so this is useful preparation rather than a detour. The king gains shelter, and the rook becomes available for central work. Neither achievement means White can stop calculating Black's active knight play.
lessons.intent: The f3 knight has competing responsibilities: it attacks d4 and defends e5. White wants more pieces participating before deciding how to resolve that tension. Castling improves the king's position and activates a rook without committing the queen to the defense of a temporary central foothold.
lessons.plan: After ...Be7, White can play Re1 and meet ...d6 with exd6. Black can recapture and prepare castling while White eventually recovers d4. Notice the order: the supplied line exchanges the vulnerable e-pawn before moving its knight defender, rather than assuming that rook support alone settles every central capture.
lessons.tactic: On f1 the rook also protects f2, so castling has an immediate defensive effect against the g4 knight. Meanwhile, both black knights still attack e5. Before sending the f3 knight to d4, calculate the resulting captures; preparing Re1 does not make that calculation unnecessary.
lessons.theme: White continues the development investment begun with Bc4. King safety and rook access now support a concrete central task, rather than serving as vague compensation for the missing pawn.
lessons.alternativeNote: Qe2 directly reinforces e5, but its supplied continuation includes ...Qe7 and a later ...f6. Castling keeps the queen uncommitted and prepares rook support instead. Compare the resulting coordination and king safety, not merely the number of defenders on e5.

lessons.title: Prepare Safety Before Opening the Center
lessons.question: Which development task should Black complete before challenging White's advanced pawn?
lessons.takeaway: The modest-looking ...Be7 clears the last piece from Black's castling route. That matters because ...d6 can lead to exchanges that open the e-file. Black does not need another immediate threat to justify this move: preparing king safety makes the coming transformation easier to handle. The two knights already give White a concrete central problem to organize against.
lessons.intent: Black's active knights contrast with the uncastled king and undeveloped kingside bishop. Bringing the bishop out reduces that development imbalance without moving the queen. It also places a piece between the king and the e-file that White's rook may soon occupy.
lessons.plan: White's main continuation is Re1, reinforcing e5. Black then challenges that pawn with ...d6, recaptures on d6, and prepares to castle. White will seek to recover d4 once the e-pawn's fate is settled. Black should value this route to coordination rather than insist on preserving the extra pawn indefinitely.
lessons.tactic: The supplied 7.Nxd4 permits ...Ngxe5. White's knight has left e5 undefended, allowing Black to exchange one extra central pawn for another. Developing the bishop has not erased that threat, which explains why White first reinforces the center instead of automatically restoring material equality.
lessons.theme: The activity race is becoming a coordination test. Black connects king preparation with central pressure, rather than asking the advanced knight to create an attack without support from the remaining pieces.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Bc5 develops more aggressively, but White can answer c3 and challenge the advanced pawn while Black still needs king safety. The quieter ...Be7 prioritizes castling readiness. Compare stability and coordination alongside the bishop's immediate activity.

lessons.title: Reinforce Before Resolving the Center
lessons.question: How can White strengthen the contested pawn without prematurely abandoning its knight defender?
lessons.takeaway: Re1 gives e5 a second defender and makes practical use of castling. The rook supports White's current center and occupies a file likely to open after a pawn exchange. Be careful about the conclusion, though: this is reinforcement, not permission to move the f3 knight regardless of Black's reply. Both black knights still attack e5, and the central tension needs resolving.
lessons.intent: White wants the rook involved before deciding the e-pawn's future. The f3 knight remains an important defender as well as a potential recapturing piece on d4. Adding rook support improves coordination, but does not turn the advanced pawn into a permanent or independently secure asset.
lessons.plan: Black's direct response is ...d6, adding another attack on e5. White can exchange with exd6 and, after ...cxd6, recover d4 with the knight. Black then seeks castling and central activity. White should recognize that exchanging the e-pawn, not simply placing a rook behind it, releases the knight from its defensive obligation.
lessons.tactic: Count the entire exchange before calling the rook a replacement defender. If the f3 knight leaves, a lone rook cannot safely trade itself for a knight on e5 while another black knight can recapture there. The supplied ...d6 and exd6 sequence avoids relying on that misleading defender count.
lessons.theme: The rook joins as a supporting piece before finding open-file work. This links White's castling with an orderly central liquidation, rather than promising that one developing move solves every pawn threat.
lessons.alternativeNote: Qe2 also reinforces e5, and its supplied line continues ...d6, exd6, and ...Qxd6. Re1 assigns that initial support to the rook while keeping the queen flexible. Immediate Nxd4 instead abandons e5 before either reinforcement or clarification.

lessons.title: Challenge the Advanced Pawn Directly
lessons.question: How can Black increase the central pressure without first weakening its own kingside shelter?
lessons.takeaway: With ...d6, Black adds a pawn attack to the pressure already exerted on e5 by both knights. White's rook reinforcement has not made the advanced pawn permanent. Exchanging it will remove White's central space and allow Black to rebuild a central foothold with the c-pawn. Black is choosing an active structural transformation rather than trying to defend the extra d4 pawn at all costs.
lessons.intent: Black wants to reduce White's space while keeping a sound route to castling. Moving the d-pawn also opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, although the knight on g4 still occupies part of that route. Central pressure and the remaining bishop's future activity are connected.
lessons.plan: White's main response is exd6, followed by ...cxd6 and Nxd4. Black can then castle and consider advancing the replacement d-pawn against the c4 bishop. White should use the clarification to restore material and finish development, while watching how Black's new central pawn can gain time against an exposed piece.
lessons.tactic: The supplied 8.Nxd4 allows ...Ngxe5. White has removed its knight defender, and Black's capturing knight on e5 is supported by both the other knight and the d6 pawn. Rook support is not enough to justify taking that knight. Resolve the pawn tension before recovering material elsewhere.
lessons.theme: Black answers rook reinforcement by changing the structure. The opening is moving from defense of an advanced White pawn toward open files and a mobile black center that both sides must understand.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...f6 also challenges e5, but exf6 and later exchanges can change Black's kingside pawn cover. The move ...d6 avoids that immediate shelter concession. Compare the structure and piece activity left after the exchange, not just which move attacks e5.

lessons.title: Release Space to Resolve the Tension
lessons.question: Should White keep defending the advanced pawn or exchange it before recovering material elsewhere?
lessons.takeaway: White plays exd6 because maintaining e5 has become more demanding than useful. The capture removes Black's d-pawn, clears the e-file in front of White's rook, and prepares a cleaner recovery of d4. White gives up the space gained earlier, but keeping that space is not an end in itself. The important gain is freeing the pieces from a difficult defensive responsibility.
lessons.intent: White transforms an attacked central pawn into open lines and a route back to material equality. Once the e-pawn is exchanged, the f3 knight can concentrate on d4. Black still chooses the recapturing unit, so White must remain flexible about the resulting pawn structure.
lessons.plan: After ...cxd6, White can recover d4 with the knight while Black retains a central pawn and prepares castling. The supplied ...Qxd6 is also possible and produces a different structure. White should inspect that choice before deciding how to develop the queenside; Black should prioritize the threatened bishop before pursuing unrelated activity.
lessons.tactic: The pawn on d6 attacks the bishop on e7. This makes recapturing urgent: the supplied ...O-O allows dxe7, after which a recapture still leaves Black having lost a bishop for the pawn. White's exchange therefore creates a concrete threat as well as clearing the center.
lessons.theme: The advanced pawn's role changes from a space-gaining unit to a means of clarification. White releases a temporary asset to make the rest of the position easier to coordinate.
lessons.alternativeNote: Immediate Nxd4 permits ...Ngxe5, preserving Black's extra pawn. Exd6 addresses the pressure first and gives White a more orderly recovery. Compare the complete sequence of exchanges rather than judging the moves only by which pawn White captures first.

lessons.title: Rebuild a Mobile Central Foothold
lessons.question: Which recapture preserves a central pawn while leaving Black's queen uncommitted?
lessons.takeaway: Black chooses ...cxd6, removing the dangerous pawn and replacing the original d-pawn with the former c-pawn. The doubled d-pawns are temporary if White now takes d4. More important is the surviving pawn's mobility: it can later advance against the c4 bishop. Judge this structure by its likely transformation, rather than treating the current doubled pawns as a lasting weakness.
lessons.intent: Black trades a queenside pawn's original role for central presence and gains a half-open c-file. Vacating c7 also makes a queen route from d8 to b6 possible once the position calls for it. White can restore material, but Black retains useful central mobility.
lessons.plan: White's straightforward continuation is Nxd4. Black can castle and later consider ...d5, especially if White attacks the g4 knight with h3. White may develop Bg5 first, as another supplied line shows. In either case, Black should connect the replacement pawn's activity with development rather than merely defend d4.
lessons.tactic: Recapturing removes the attack on e7 and avoids the material loss shown after premature castling. Black's queen remains on d8, so the capture is not an early queen sortie. The next calculation concerns central knight exchanges and which recapturing piece would benefit from an opened d-file.
lessons.theme: The original central pawns are disappearing, but central play continues. Black's c-pawn assumes a new role that will connect a later bishop attack with a broader central initiative.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Qxd6 avoids the doubled-pawn snapshot and activates the queen; White then has b3 in the sample continuation. With ...cxd6, Black keeps the queen back and retains a pawn advance. Compare future central mobility with immediate queen activity.

lessons.title: Recover Material After Resolving Duties
lessons.question: Can White now recover the advanced pawn without abandoning another central pawn's defense?
lessons.takeaway: Nxd4 restores material equality and places the knight in the center. The timing matters: White no longer has an e5 pawn that needs this knight's protection. The opening's delayed recovery is complete, but Black still has counterplay. The centralized knight meets its counterpart on c6, while the d6 pawn can advance against White's bishop on c4.
lessons.intent: White converts the temporary development investment into equal material and central piece activity. The position is now less about a missing pawn and more about how White's active pieces meet Black's mobile center. The queenside pieces still need development despite the attractive knight post.
lessons.plan: Black can castle, after which White may question the g4 knight with h3 or support d4 with c3. Black should keep ...d5 in mind because it attacks the bishop, not the knight. If Black exchanges knights immediately with ...Nxd4, the supplied continuation gives White a central queen recapture.
lessons.tactic: The c6 knight attacks d4, but White's queen can recapture after ...Nxd4; the centralized knight is not simply hanging. The d6 pawn does not currently attack d4. Distinguish the possible knight exchange from the later pawn advance, whose direct target is White's bishop on c4.
lessons.theme: The delayed recapture has served its purpose. The lesson now shifts toward the interaction between White's bishop, the central knights, and Black's ability to answer wing threats with central action.
lessons.alternativeNote: Bg5 is also supplied and develops the other bishop before Nxd4 appears later. Immediate recovery is not uniquely forced. Compare the concrete value of that extra developing move with the simplicity of restoring material and occupying the center now.

lessons.title: Secure the King Before Counterplay
lessons.question: What preparation makes Black's coming central challenge easier to conduct safely?
lessons.takeaway: Black castles before launching the next central challenge. White's rook occupies the e-file, so leaving the king behind the e7 bishop would complicate future piece moves and exchanges. Castling removes that concern and brings a rook to f8. The f-pawn still blocks that rook's activity, but Black now has a safer foundation for the central counterstroke.
lessons.intent: Black combines king safety with preparation for active play. White has developed pieces and an open rook file, while Black has a mobile central pawn and a knight near White's king. Removing the king from e8 makes it easier to use those assets without defensive distractions.
lessons.plan: White can play h3 against the g4 knight, but Black can consider ...d5 against the c4 bishop instead of automatically retreating. White may also exchange on c6 or support d4 with c3. Black should compare these structures before choosing a central advance, a knight retreat, or an exchange.
lessons.tactic: Castling does not create an immediate rook attack against f2 because Black's own f-pawn blocks the file. Its tactical value is preparatory. After h3 and ...d5, both sides have attacked pieces, and Black can calculate the resulting exchanges without keeping the king behind the e7 bishop.
lessons.theme: Both kings are now castled, but the position is not becoming quiet or symmetrical. Black's replacement central pawn is about to turn the development phase into another exchange of concrete threats.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied immediate ...d5 also challenges the bishop and can be followed by castling. Castling first emphasizes safety while preserving that option. Immediate ...Nxd4 instead releases the knight tension and lets White recapture with the queen, creating a different central arrangement.

lessons.title: Question the Knight Without Assuming Retreat
lessons.question: Can White challenge the advanced knight, and what central counterattack must be checked first?
lessons.takeaway: The move h3 asks Black's g4 knight to justify its advanced post. That is useful, but it does not guarantee a retreat: ...d5 attacks White's c4 bishop in return. White must compare the resulting exchanges before counting a gained tempo. The pawn move also leaves h2 empty, a detail that becomes important if Black's bishop later reaches d6.
lessons.intent: White wants to reduce pressure near the king while preserving the active central knight. The cost is another move before queenside development and a change to the king's pawn cover. Black's mobile central pawn offers a concrete challenge to White's intended gain of time.
lessons.plan: Against ...d5, White can exchange on c6 before relocating the bishop, as the repertoire does. Black may instead retreat with ...Nf6, when Bb3 appears in the supplied continuation. White should adapt to the actual response; Black should compare a straightforward retreat with the competing threat against the bishop.
lessons.tactic: After ...d5, hxg4 is not a free piece. The supplied continuation runs ...Nxd4, Qxd4, ...dxc4, and Qxc4. White captures both black knights, but loses its central knight and c4 bishop during the exchanges. Count all the minor pieces before deciding what the pawn attack has achieved.
lessons.theme: An attack on a knight again meets a possible central counterattack. Unlike the earlier e-pawn push, this move also changes the king shelter and creates a future entry square for Black.
lessons.alternativeNote: Nxc6 first clarifies the central knights and uses h3 afterward, while c3 reinforces d4 before Black's advance. These are different reasonable priorities. The repertoire questions the knight immediately, accepting that Black may answer through the center rather than retreat.

lessons.title: Answer a Wing Threat Centrally
lessons.question: Can Black create a competing threat instead of immediately moving the attacked knight?
lessons.takeaway: Black's ...d5 attacks the c4 bishop and changes the meaning of h3. The g4 knight remains attacked, but White now has a piece under pressure too. This is the practical value of preserving a mobile central pawn. Black gains space and asks White to calculate competing captures instead of simply enjoying a tempo against the knight.
lessons.intent: Black uses central mobility to resist a wing pawn's attempt to drive the knight backward. The exposed c4 bishop is the immediate target, while the central knights can also exchange. This is a specific counterattack based on the board, not permission to ignore attacked pieces generally.
lessons.plan: White's repertoire response is Nxc6, followed by ...bxc6 and Bd3. That changes the pawn structure before saving the bishop. White can also retreat immediately with Bf1. Black should compare the resulting king exposure and minor-piece balance before deciding whether the g4 knight should withdraw or continue creating threats.
lessons.tactic: The supplied hxg4 line shows why the counterattack works: ...Nxd4 exchanges the central knights, then Qxd4 permits ...dxc4 against the bishop. White can answer Qxc4, but has exchanged two minor pieces for Black's two knights rather than won an uncontested knight on g4.
lessons.theme: The pawn created by ...cxd6 now earns its central role. Black turns the earlier structural transformation into active resistance, forcing White to reorganize before claiming a comfortable development advantage.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Nf6 accepts the pawn attack and returns the knight to a conventional square; White then has Bb3. That is simpler, but asks less of White immediately. Compare a secure retreat with the concrete exchange possibilities created by ...d5.

lessons.title: Exchange with a Queen Threat
lessons.question: How can White clarify the central knights before committing the attacked bishop to a retreat?
lessons.takeaway: Nxc6 removes Black's central knight and attacks the queen on d8. That threat gives the exchange urgency even though White's bishop is still attacked by the d5 pawn. After ...bxc6, White can address the bishop. The trade resolves one tactical problem, but also gives Black connected central pawns rather than the doubled c-pawns familiar from some other opening positions.
lessons.intent: White uses a forcing capture to simplify the competing attacks. Black's original c-pawn has already reached d5, so the expected b-pawn recapture creates a new supporting pawn on c6. White gains clarification, not an automatic structural advantage or a permanently weak black center.
lessons.plan: Black's sound supplied response is ...bxc6, eliminating the knight's threats and restoring material. White then moves the c4 bishop, with Bd3 continuing this line. Black should use c6 to support d5 and look for bishop activity; White must complete development without overlooking the remaining g4 knight's access to f2.
lessons.tactic: From c6 the knight attacks both the queen on d8 and bishop on e7. The supplied ...Bc5 allows Nxd8, while ...Nxf2 permits Nxe7+ and further forcing captures. The check in the latter line matters: Black cannot assume its own threat against the queen will arrive first.
lessons.theme: White untangles the competing attacks through a forcing exchange. The resulting black pawn center is a genuine asset to reckon with, not merely damage inflicted by a routine knight trade.
lessons.alternativeNote: Bf1 saves the bishop immediately and retains the central knight tension. Nxc6 changes the structure first while attacking the queen. Compare whether keeping the knights helps White or leaves Black more forcing captures around d4 and f2.

lessons.title: Recapture into a Connected Center
lessons.question: How can Black remove the knight's threats while preserving the attack on White's bishop?
lessons.takeaway: The recapture ...bxc6 restores material and removes the knight attacking Black's queen. It also creates connected pawns on c6 and d5, with the former supporting the latter. These are not doubled c-pawns: the original c-pawn is on d5. White's bishop remains attacked, so Black solves the immediate tactical problem without giving up the central pressure.
lessons.intent: Black accepts a changed queenside structure in exchange for a supported center. The b-file becomes half-open, and the queen retains its route through c7. The urgent task is removing the knight's threats; the useful pawn structure is a consequence, not a substitute for that calculation.
lessons.plan: White can preserve the bishop with Bd3. Black then chooses between retreating the attacked g4 knight and creating a sharper threat with ...Bd6. In quieter supplied lines, ...c5 and ...Bb7 develop the center and bishop together. White should watch those active possibilities rather than assume the new c6 pawn is weak.
lessons.tactic: Trying ...Nxf2 before recapturing allows the supplied Nxe7+ sequence, where White uses checks and rook activity before Black's counterattack can justify itself. Recapturing first removes that dangerous knight. The g4 knight is still attacked, but White must also account for ...dxc4 against its bishop.
lessons.theme: Two pawn recaptures have produced Black's mobile center. Tracking the pawns' actual origins prevents a misleading structural lesson and explains why Black can seek active play rather than defend lasting weaknesses.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied attempts to ignore the knight, including ...Bc5 and ...Nxf2, allow forcing material losses. Prioritize the queen threat here. The value of ...bxc6 is concrete: it removes the dangerous piece while retaining the attack on White's bishop.

lessons.title: Preserve the Bishop Without Relaxing
lessons.question: How can White save the attacked bishop while staying alert to Black's access near the king?
lessons.takeaway: Bd3 removes the bishop from the d5 pawn's attack and retains a diagonal toward h7. That solves a real problem, but it does not establish a comfortable White position. Black can answer ...Bd6, combining the bishop with the g4 knight against the empty h2 square. White must now evaluate king safety afresh instead of treating the active-looking retreat as the start of its own attack.
lessons.intent: White keeps both bishops rather than exchanging the c4 bishop for the g4 knight. Black, however, has a supported center and pieces close to the king. With White's queenside still undeveloped, preserving attacking potential cannot take priority over recognizing Black's more immediate threats.
lessons.plan: If Black retreats with ...Nf6, White can develop Nd2 in a relatively quieter setting. Against ...Bd6, that development faces ...Bh2+ and a much sharper king-safety problem. Black should compare retreat with coordinated pressure; White must distinguish these branches rather than apply the same comfortable development story to both.
lessons.tactic: The bishop is no longer exposed to ...dxc4, but f2 remains accessible to Black's knight. The packet distinguishes immediate ...Nxf2 from first playing ...Bd6 and arranging a protected bishop check. Calculate the attacking pieces together: access to a target alone does not make every sacrifice sound.
lessons.theme: Central clarification gives way to king safety. White preserves an active bishop, but Black's coordinated reply can seize the initiative; the narrative must follow those concrete threats rather than the side with more developed-looking pieces.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied hxg4 allows ...dxc4 and exchanges White's bishop for Black's knight, followed by Qf3 for activity. Bd3 keeps the bishop instead. Compare the resulting minor pieces and king exposure, not merely which attacked piece White saves or captures first.

lessons.title: Coordinate Before Offering the Knight
lessons.question: Can Black turn the knight's contact with White's shelter into a coordinated king threat?
lessons.takeaway: Black's ...Bd6 aims along the clear diagonal to h2. The g4 knight protects that entry square, so a bishop check there would not be an undefended incursion. This makes the attack more dangerous than a knight sacrifice alone. White may still develop, but must calculate how a protected check changes the king's options before deciding that the attacked knight can simply be collected.
lessons.intent: Black coordinates bishop and knight against the square vacated by h3. The knight remains under pawn attack, so this is a concrete decision to create counterthreats, not a leisurely improvement. The bishop's access must justify keeping the knight forward instead of saving it immediately.
lessons.plan: The repertoire continues Nd2 and ...Bh2+, after which White must choose a king move and examine ...Nxf2. White also has Qe2 in the packet, with a different arrangement after ...Ne5. Black should compare the resulting defenses rather than assume that the same sacrifice works against every setup.
lessons.tactic: The resource is ...Bh2+, protected by the knight on g4. White's king cannot capture the bishop on h2 while that knight controls it. Black uses the check to change the king's position before offering the knight on f2; reversing that order gives White different defensive choices.
lessons.theme: The central phase has left Black ready for a direct attack. White's earlier h-pawn advance now matters concretely because the vacated square can host a bishop protected by another attacking piece.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Nf6 retreats the attacked knight and leads toward quieter development with ...c5 and ...Bb7. The move ...Bd6 keeps the tension and creates a forcing problem. Immediate ...Nxf2 lacks that preparatory bishop check and must be evaluated separately.

lessons.title: Develop While Preparing to Defend
lessons.question: How can White bring the remaining knight into play without overlooking Black's forcing king threats?
lessons.takeaway: Nd2 develops White's remaining knight, giving it possible routes toward f3, f1, or b3 as the position changes. It does not neutralize Black's attack: ...Bh2+ still forces the king to move. White needs another piece participating, but this is defensive organization under pressure, not a comfortable completion of the opening. The king response must be considered before making the natural developing move.
lessons.intent: White's lagging queenside development contrasts with Black's coordinated bishop and knight near the king. The knight gains future defensive options without controlling h2 or interrupting the bishop's diagonal. White is improving its resources while accepting that Black dictates the immediate pace through forcing moves.
lessons.plan: After ...Bh2+, White's more resilient supplied response is Kf1, followed by calculation of ...Nxf2. Black should compare that forcing order with quieter knight moves. If Black instead chooses ...Ne5, the packet gives Nf3 and a possible exchange on d3, illustrating a different use for the newly developed knight.
lessons.tactic: The diagonal d6-e5-f4-g3-h2 remains clear after Nd2, and the g4 knight still protects h2. Development therefore does not stop the check. Also distinguish ...Nxf2 immediately from ...Bh2+ first: the supplied continuations lead to different king positions and different opportunities for the queen.
lessons.theme: Development remains valuable, but it is no longer enough by itself. White must combine bringing pieces into play with concrete defensive calculation while Black's threats determine the next few decisions.
lessons.alternativeNote: Qe2 develops the queen first, with ...Ne5 and Be3 in its supplied continuation. Neither route establishes easy equality in the packet. Compare how each arrangement handles checks and coordinates the remaining pieces rather than choosing by a development slogan.

lessons.title: Displace the King Before Sacrificing
lessons.question: Which forcing action changes White's king position before Black commits the knight?
lessons.takeaway: The check ...Bh2+ sends the bishop into the square vacated by White's h-pawn. The g4 knight protects it, preventing the king from simply capturing. Black is not taking a pawn here; the purpose is to displace the king before acting against f2. That move order changes the coming forks and sharply reduces White's comfortable defensive choices.
lessons.intent: Black wants a king displacement rather than immediate material gain. The protected bishop check makes White choose between two very different king squares. The knight's access to f2 then becomes more forcing, while the queen remains available to exploit the resulting exposure.
lessons.plan: White should compare Kf1 with Kh1 concretely. The repertoire chooses Kf1, after which Black continues ...Nxf2 and can bring the queen into the attack if White captures. Black must maintain the connection between the bishop check and the follow-up rather than assume the advanced bishop is automatically useful forever.
lessons.tactic: After Kh1, the supplied ...Nxf2+ forks the king on h1 and queen on d1. White can capture the bishop with Kxh2, but ...Nxd1 then takes the queen. Kf1 avoids that checking fork, although it still leaves White facing a dangerous capture and sacrifice on f2.
lessons.theme: The attack depends on move order rather than a single sacrifice. Black first changes the king's square, then uses the knight's existing access under more favorable circumstances for the attacking pieces.
lessons.alternativeNote: Immediate ...Nxf2 is also supplied, but Kxf2 and ...Qh4+ produce a different defensive sequence. The bishop check first is more testing in the packet. Compare the available king moves and queen checks after each order, not just the sacrificed material.

lessons.title: Avoid the Checking Fork
lessons.question: Which king escape avoids giving Black a knight check that simultaneously attacks the queen?
lessons.takeaway: Kf1 is a defensive concession: White leaves the castled shelter because the bishop check must be answered. The crucial detail is avoiding the corner, where ...Nxf2+ would attack king and queen together. Moving inward does not make White safe, but it preserves the option to remove the knight. Choose the escape square by calculation rather than its sheltered appearance.
lessons.intent: White must answer a protected bishop check without allowing a decisive fork. On f1 the king is not checked by a knight arriving on f2. That distinction gives White a way to eliminate the knight instead of losing the queen while answering check.
lessons.plan: Black's main continuation is ...Nxf2, attacking the queen and d3 bishop. White then evaluates Kxf2 and the queen check that follows. Black could retreat the knight instead, but would release some pressure. White should focus on preserving defensive resources rather than immediately trying to punish the bishop's advanced position.
lessons.tactic: Kh1 permits ...Nxf2+, and after Kxh2 the supplied ...Nxd1 wins the queen before White recaptures the knight. On f1, White is not checked by the knight on f2 and can capture it directly. That avoids the fork's worst consequence, though the king's new exposure remains serious.
lessons.theme: White begins the defensive king journey that defines the remaining line. Familiar preferences for keeping a king near the corner must give way to the actual checks and forks available.
lessons.alternativeNote: Kh1 looks more consistent with staying sheltered, but the supplied checking fork makes it much worse. Kf1 is preferable for a specific tactical reason, not because centralizing a middlegame king is generally desirable. Visual shelter and actual safety differ here.

lessons.title: Trade the Knight for King Exposure
lessons.question: How can Black make White choose between material damage and exposing the king further?
lessons.takeaway: The capture ...Nxf2 removes a pawn and attacks both the queen on d1 and bishop on d3. White can take the knight with the king, but Black then has a queen check to continue the pursuit. This is a material investment for initiative, not a free pawn. The fork makes declining the offer uncomfortable as well.
lessons.intent: Black converts the advanced knight into access to White's king. Removing the f-pawn weakens the shelter, while the double attack makes White address the knight immediately. Compensation depends on active queen and bishop play, so the continuation matters more than the attractiveness of the sacrifice itself.
lessons.plan: After Kxf2, Black's key continuation is ...Qb6+, keeping White from consolidating. White can move the queen instead, but the supplied Qf3 allows ...Nxd3. Both sides should compare the exposed king after acceptance with the loss of a developed bishop if the knight remains on the board.
lessons.tactic: The capture is not check against the king on f1. Its forcing character comes from attacking d1 and d3 together. If White plays Kxf2, the open diagonal b6-c5-d4-e3-f2 allows the queen to check. Calculate that follow-up before treating the offered knight as a successful attack.
lessons.theme: The knight chased from f6 now gives itself up to remove White's shelter. Black's initiative passes from minor-piece coordination to queen-led pursuit, while White needs to turn extra material into defense.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Ne5 keeps the knight and can exchange it for the d3 bishop in a more conventional position. The sacrifice is more ambitious because it exposes the king. Compare the forcing continuation and White's defensive choices, rather than assuming material preservation is automatically better.

lessons.title: Accept Material Without Assuming Safety
lessons.question: Should White eliminate the forking knight or move the queen and allow another developed piece to fall?
lessons.takeaway: Kxf2 removes the knight attacking White's queen and bishop. White is now a knight ahead for a pawn, but the king stands exposed with Black ready to activate the queen. This is the more resilient supplied response, not a refutation of the sacrifice. The material can help only if White survives the forcing continuation and coordinates the remaining pieces.
lessons.intent: White chooses king exposure over the damage caused by leaving the forking knight alive. Extra minor-piece material is balanced against Black's bishops, queen access, and the missing f-pawn. Defensive planning must now prioritize legal escape routes and useful interpositions instead of relying on the material count.
lessons.plan: Black should examine ...Qb6+ immediately, and White must compare forward escape with retreat or interposition. Slower black moves give White chances to develop and reorganize; the supplied ...c5 branch includes Nf3 and a later Kf1. That contrast explains why Black's next move is a critical part of the sacrifice.
lessons.tactic: The capture is legal because no black piece currently defends f2. In particular, the rook on f8 is blocked by its own f7 pawn. The next issue is ...Qb6+ along the clear diagonal to f2. Removing the knight ends the fork, not the calculation.
lessons.theme: White's opening initiative has become a defensive task. The piece count favors White, but Black's ability to keep the king exposed determines whether that extra material will become useful.
lessons.alternativeNote: Qf3 saves the queen but permits ...Nxd3, losing the developed bishop while Black retains the knight. Kxf2 removes the attacker completely. Compare the surviving defensive pieces and Black's checks rather than judging the king capture only by its unusual appearance.

lessons.title: Make the Sacrifice Count with Check
lessons.question: How can Black prevent White from using its extra piece to consolidate?
lessons.takeaway: The queen check ...Qb6+ is the critical continuation of Black's material investment. It reaches f2 along an open diagonal and forces White to address king safety immediately. A slower move would offer time to organize the extra knight. Earlier pawn play matters here: vacating c7 gave the queen its route from d8, and the checking diagonal is still clear.
lessons.intent: Black needs forcing activity because the knight has already been sacrificed. The queen joins the attack before White can settle the king or coordinate its pieces. The relevant imbalance is continuing access to the king against White's extra material and potential defensive development.
lessons.plan: White's more resilient supplied response is Kf3, although Re3 can interpose. Black can then extend the attack with central pawn play rather than search only for checks. White should evaluate queen entry squares and the h2 bishop's support before choosing a retreat that merely looks closer to home.
lessons.tactic: The checking diagonal is b6-c5-d4-e3-f2. Retreating with Kf1 allows the supplied ...Qg1+, where the bishop on h2 protects the queen's entry square. That cooperation explains why moving backward is dangerous; White must evaluate the queen and bishop together rather than the current check alone.
lessons.theme: The queen exploits routes made available by earlier pawn exchanges. Black's attack is therefore connected to the central transformation, rather than an isolated trick appearing after an otherwise unrelated opening.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Qh4+ also checks, but White can return to f1 and develop defensive resources in that continuation. The move ...Qb6+ creates a different escape problem. Compare the resulting king positions and supported queen entries, not simply the fact that both moves check.

lessons.title: Choose the Least Dangerous Exposure
lessons.question: Which escape avoids Black's strongest queen entry despite taking the king farther into the board?
lessons.takeaway: Kf3 looks alarming, and White would not choose this king position without a concrete reason. Here it avoids the dangerous retreat to f1, where ...Qg1+ brings the queen close with bishop support. White is choosing among difficult defensive options, not advancing the king for activity. The next task is to create breathing room while getting more pieces involved.
lessons.intent: White must leave the queen's diagonal without allowing a stronger forcing continuation. The king remains exposed, while the extra knight and undeveloped pieces offer potential defensive resources. The move accepts a lasting coordination problem in order to avoid more immediate tactical damage.
lessons.plan: Black's repertoire continuation is ...c5, expanding the center and clearing a lateral queen route. White can answer g3 to reshape the king's surroundings. Another supplied branch uses ...Qd4 and Re3. White should choose the defensive setup in response to Black's actual attack rather than assume the forward king move has solved the danger.
lessons.tactic: In the supplied Kf1 line, ...Qg1+ is supported by the h2 bishop, so White cannot simply capture the invading queen. Re3 instead blocks the current diagonal but allows ...f5. Compare those concrete resources before dismissing Kf3 solely because a middlegame king normally belongs behind pawns.
lessons.theme: The defensive king journey reaches its most unusual square. From here, pawn moves must be evaluated by the attacking lines they obstruct and the escape routes they create, not by ordinary opening habits.
lessons.alternativeNote: Re3 keeps the king on f2 but commits the rook to interposition, with ...f5 in the supplied response. Kf3 leaves the rook available while exposing the king farther. Compare the complete defensive arrangement and Black's follow-up, not just the king's rank.

lessons.title: Improve the Attack Without Checking
lessons.question: How can Black add attacking options without immediately moving another piece toward the king?
lessons.takeaway: The move ...c5 clears c6 for the queen's lateral route toward the kingside and prepares ...c4 against the d3 bishop. Black pauses the checks to improve the attack's reach. There is a tradeoff: the pawn now blocks the queen's old diagonal from b6 toward f2. The new routes and central threats matter more here than preserving every existing line.
lessons.intent: Black uses the connected central pawns to interfere with White's defensive organization. Advancing this pawn gains control of d4 and makes another advance against the bishop possible. Clearing c6 also lets the queen move across the sixth rank, creating a fresh direction of attack.
lessons.plan: White's main supplied response is g3, after which Black can activate the c8 bishop with ...Bxh3. Immediate Nf1 instead meets ...Qf6+ in the sample line. White must account for both the queen's new route and ...c4 against the bishop; Black should exploit whichever problem White's defensive choice leaves unresolved.
lessons.tactic: After 17.Nf1, ...Qf6+ uses the cleared route b6-c6-d6-e6-f6 and checks down the f-file toward f3. The supplied continuation then includes ...Re8+ and central pawn action. This is why a nonchecking pawn move can demand an immediate defensive response rather than grant White a free developing tempo.
lessons.theme: The attack expands from a sequence of checks into control over the defender's choices. Pawns created by earlier recaptures now chase pieces and clear new queen routes around the exposed king.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Bc7 withdraws the h2 bishop, but White can answer Re7 and gain active rook play. The move ...c5 keeps the bishop forward while improving other attackers. Compare whether retreat is necessary with the concrete pressure maintained by central action.

lessons.title: Create Breathing Room at a Cost
lessons.question: Can White improve nearby escape options without immediately opening the most dangerous attacking lines?
lessons.takeaway: The move g3 controls f4 and h4, blocks the h2 bishop's diagonal beyond g3, and vacates g2 as a possible escape square. Those are useful defensive changes, not a complete shelter. Black can answer ...Bxh3, activating the other bishop and controlling g2 again. White is creating possibilities in a difficult position while accepting that each pawn move has a cost.
lessons.intent: White needs useful squares around the exposed king more urgently than routine development. Advancing the g-pawn changes pawn control and bishop access, but also stops defending h3. That concession lets Black activate the c8 bishop with a capture rather than spend a quiet developing tempo.
lessons.plan: After ...Bxh3, White can reorganize the knight, with Nb3 in the repertoire and Nf1 in another supplied line. Black should combine the bishops with central or f-pawn advances. White must reassess g2 after the bishop capture; vacating a square does not guarantee the king will be able to use it.
lessons.tactic: The g3 pawn blocks the diagonal from h2 toward f4, but the other bishop has a clear route from c8 through d7, e6, f5, and g4 to h3. That capture is no longer subject to gxh3 because White's pawn has left g2. Track the two bishops separately.
lessons.theme: White reshapes the remaining shelter around an already exposed king. Each pawn move gains some control while surrendering something else, so the defense becomes a series of limited, concrete concessions.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied g4 also clears g2, but leaves the h2 bishop's diagonal unobstructed and meets ...c4 against the d3 bishop. Moving one square retains control of f4. Compare the precise lines and squares changed, not merely whether both moves create space.

lessons.title: Activate the Bishop and Restrict Escape
lessons.question: How can Black exploit White's pawn move to involve the remaining bishop and restrict the king?
lessons.takeaway: With ...Bxh3, Black's remaining bishop joins the attack while taking a pawn. Its route is clear because the d-pawn moved earlier and the g4 knight has been sacrificed. From h3 it controls g2 and f1, reducing White's routes back toward shelter. The capture matters, but the restriction of the king is what makes this development especially useful.
lessons.intent: Black gains a second pawn for the sacrificed knight and brings the bishop into an active role. White remains ahead by a minor piece, but its king is the immediate target. Restricting escape squares gives Black time to introduce pawns and rooks into the attack.
lessons.plan: White's repertoire response is Nb3, clearing d2 for the queen while pressuring c5. Black can then play ...f5 and prepare further pawn-supported threats. Nf1 is another supplied defense, with ...Bg1 as a possible reply. Black should coordinate new forces with the bishops rather than expect those two pieces to finish alone.
lessons.tactic: There is no immediate g-pawn recapture on h3: that pawn now stands on g3, not g2. The bishop also controls g2 directly, removing the escape option White just created. Exact pawn placement turns an apparent bishop sacrifice into a straightforward capture with an important defensive restriction.
lessons.theme: Black's attack now includes both bishops. Earlier central clearance and White's latest defensive concession combine to develop the remaining minor piece with tempo in the broader struggle over king safety.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...c4 attacks the d3 bishop first, but White has Bxh7+ and a possible king escape in that branch. Capturing h3 immediately controls g2. Compare which order restricts the king most effectively before spending time against another piece.

lessons.title: Clear a Route for the Queen
lessons.question: How can White improve coordination while keeping Black's central pawn advances in view?
lessons.takeaway: Nb3 sends the knight away from the king, but does not abandon the defense. It frees d2 for the queen, attacks c5, and controls d4. White needs coordinated counterpressure, not simply a crowd of pieces near the king. The intended Qd2 can challenge the bishop on h2 along the now-clear second rank, giving Black something concrete to consider.
lessons.intent: White uses its extra knight to support a workable defensive arrangement. Vacating d2 gives the queen an active post and also opens the c1 bishop's diagonal. Pressure on c5 is useful, but taking that pawn must remain secondary to checking Black's forcing resources against king and queen.
lessons.plan: Black's main supplied reply is ...f5, after which White plays Qd2. Black can instead use ...c4 against the d3 bishop, when Bf4 appears in the sample continuation. White should coordinate the queen and bishops while Black compares central tempo gains with pawn-supported threats closer to the king.
lessons.tactic: Once d2 is clear, the queen can reach the second rank and attack h2 through e2, f2, and g2. A clear capture route is not a guarantee that capturing will be safe: Black may answer with checks or pawn breaks. The knight move prepares a threat, not an immediate material win.
lessons.theme: White moves from emergency king moves toward organized resistance. The extra knight helps make space for other defenders, while central pressure gives White something useful beyond simply enduring the attack.
lessons.alternativeNote: Nf1 also clears d2 and puts the knight nearer the king, but ...Bg1 keeps Black active in the supplied response. Nb3 instead adds central influence. Compare the knight's concrete tasks and the resulting queen activity, not just its distance from the king.

lessons.title: Support the Next Wave of Threats
lessons.question: How can Black reinforce its attacking pieces before White coordinates against the advanced bishops?
lessons.takeaway: The advance ...f5 supports a bishop check on g4 and prepares ...f4 against White's g3 pawn. That gives the attack new force before White coordinates with Qd2. The rook on f8 is not attacking the king yet: its own pawn still blocks the file. Black is preparing the conditions for rook activity rather than claiming that the file is already open.
lessons.intent: Black wants pawn support for the bishops and a way to involve the rooks. White's exposed king makes control of checking squares especially valuable. The move loosens Black's own pawn shelter, but creates immediate practical threats that White must address before collecting central pawns.
lessons.plan: White's main response is Qd2, challenging the h2 bishop and moving the queen out of a tactical alignment. Black then compares ...f4 with rook activation on e8, both supplied ideas. White should avoid treating the knight's attack on c5 as a free pawn while Black has forcing checks available.
lessons.tactic: The supplied 19.Nxc5 allows ...Bg4+, when Kg2 permits ...Bxd1 against the queen. The new f5 pawn protects the checking bishop on g4, so the king cannot simply take it. This turns a potential bishop sortie into a concrete skewer and explains why White needs preparation.
lessons.theme: The attack gains a second wave after the knight sacrifice and bishop deployment. Pawn support makes the remaining pieces more effective and prevents White from converting central pressure into effortless consolidation.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...c4 immediately attacks the d3 bishop, while ...Rae8 activates a rook on the open e-file. The move ...f5 prioritizes supported threats near the king. Compare White's strongest defense to each; the bounded lines do not make one continuation compulsory.

lessons.title: Defend by Creating a Concrete Threat
lessons.question: How can White improve queen safety while making Black account for an exposed attacking piece?
lessons.takeaway: Qd2 uses the square cleared by the knight to attack the bishop on h2 along the second rank. It also removes the queen from d1, where ...Bg4+ could skewer it behind the king. White is improving coordination through a real threat rather than waiting passively. Black can still answer ...f4, so the prospective bishop capture must be weighed against fresh king threats.
lessons.intent: White needs queen activity that reduces tactical vulnerability and challenges Black's attackers. Moving off d1 breaks the specific alignment behind the king on f3. Attacking h2 also asks Black to justify leaving a bishop exposed instead of allowing the attack to continue without any counterpressure.
lessons.plan: Black's repertoire reply is ...f4, counterattacking g3 rather than automatically saving the bishop. White then compares advancing the pawn with captures that open lines. Another supplied continuation uses ...Rae8 and rook exchanges before Qxh2. White must reassess the capture after each reply instead of treating the queen threat as a settled gain.
lessons.tactic: The route d2-e2-f2-g2-h2 is clear, so Qxh2 is a genuine threat. Separately, moving the queen avoids the ...Bg4+ and ...Bxd1 sequence shown against Nxc5. Black's bishop check can remain dangerous, but it no longer wins a queen waiting on d1 behind the king.
lessons.theme: White's defense finally asks a concrete question about an attacking piece. The next phase tests whether that counterpressure slows Black down or whether a pawn break creates a more urgent obligation.
lessons.alternativeNote: Kf2 is supplied as a direct attempt to improve the king's position, but does not create the same threat against h2. Qd2 combines queen safety and counterpressure. Compare how much useful work each defensive move performs while respecting Black's checks and pawn breaks.

lessons.title: Attack the Pawn Cover Before Retreating
lessons.question: Can Black meet the threat to its bishop with a more urgent attack on White's remaining cover?
lessons.takeaway: Black plays ...f4 instead of immediately saving the h2 bishop. The pawn attacks g3 and threatens a capture that would uncover the f8 rook against White's king. White cannot judge Qxh2 as a simple material gain without calculating that reply. The advanced pawn is itself defended by the rook, so removing the pawn also requires attention to forcing recaptures.
lessons.intent: Black wants to turn pawn contact into open lines toward the king. The h2 bishop may be expendable if its capture allows a stronger continuation. The imbalance remains material against activity, but the rook is now ready to participate as soon as the blocking f-pawn moves aside.
lessons.plan: White's more resilient supplied continuation is g4, avoiding the immediate opening of the f-file. Black can then use ...h5 as a second pawn lever. White must also calculate captures on f4 and h2; Black should verify the resulting checks rather than assume that any offered bishop is justified by the king's exposure.
lessons.tactic: After gxf4, the supplied ...Rxf4+ forces White to reckon with the rook, and Qxf4 allows ...Bxf4 from h2 through the vacated g3 square. After Qxh2 instead, ...fxg3+ uncovers a rook check down the f-file. The pawn on g3 does not itself check the king on f3.
lessons.theme: Black answers counterpressure by attacking the remaining pawn cover. Pawn exchanges can now activate the rook, extending the initiative beyond the bishops that originally helped drive White's king into the open.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Bg4+ checks immediately, but its continuation lets White head toward g2 and later take the h2 bishop. The move ...f4 first threatens to change the structure. Compare the position after a check, not merely the appeal of forcing a king move.

lessons.title: Leave the Attacking Rook Obstructed
lessons.question: How can White respond to the pawn contact without opening the rook's direct line toward the king?
lessons.takeaway: The advance g4 avoids exchanging on f4 and leaves Black's own pawn blocking the rook's line toward f3. This is a defensive achievement, not proof that the king is safe. The g4 pawn becomes a target for ...h5, and the h2 bishop's diagonal is now clear. White chooses a temporary obstruction over captures that immediately accelerate the attack.
lessons.intent: White needs to keep the f8 rook from gaining direct access to the king. Advancing the g-pawn avoids both ...fxg3 and the forcing exchanges after gxf4. This improvised defense remains vulnerable to another pawn lever and does not remove the need for active piece coordination.
lessons.plan: Black's main continuation is ...h5, challenging g4 from a second direction. White can then consider Qxh2 but must calculate the checking pawn capture that follows. Black also has ...Bg3 in the packet. White should compare the lines each reply opens and the escape squares left available, rather than seek a permanent shelter here.
lessons.tactic: The supplied gxf4 permits ...Rxf4+, Qxf4, and ...Bxf4, with the bishop crossing the vacated g3 square. Advancing avoids that immediate liquidation, but does not make the new pawn safe. After ...h5, ...hxg4+ would check the king directly with the capturing pawn.
lessons.theme: White's defense depends on maintaining temporary obstructions rather than rebuilding a conventional shelter. Black can attack the new pawn target from another direction, so closing one route does not end the initiative.
lessons.alternativeNote: Capturing with gxf4 removes an attacking pawn but opens the supplied rook-and-bishop sequence at a heavy cost. The quieter g4 leaves that pawn alive because it also obstructs Black's rook. Compare the lines a capture opens, not just the unit removed.

lessons.title: Use a Second Pawn Lever
lessons.question: How can Black challenge White's new pawn barrier while preserving the pressure from the advanced f-pawn?
lessons.takeaway: The move ...h5 attacks White's g4 pawn from another direction. White avoided opening the f-file, but Black can now capture the new barrier with check. That creates a reason to leave the h2 bishop under attack: Black may gain more from continuing the king pursuit than from saving it. The open e-file gives the rooks another route into the attack.
lessons.intent: Black undermines the pawn White advanced to avoid the first break. The f4 pawn still controls squares near the king, while the h-pawn creates a fresh capture on g4. Coordinated pawn levers and potential rook activity now carry the attack alongside the remaining bishop threats.
lessons.plan: The supplied continuation is Qxh2, ...hxg4+, Ke2, and ...Rae8+, bringing the queenside rook into the pursuit. White should calculate this before taking the bishop and look for chances to exchange attackers. Black must maintain coordination: the continuation shows serious pressure and rook exchanges, not a demonstrated forced mate.
lessons.tactic: After Qxh2, ...hxg4+ checks with the pawn itself, which attacks f3 from g4. If the king chooses e2, ...Rae8+ checks along the clear e-file above White's rook on e1. This differs from ...fxg3+ earlier, where the check would have come from the uncovered f8 rook.
lessons.theme: The line ends with the attack expanding through another pawn contact. White's attempt to avoid one opening of lines creates a new target, showing how structural changes can sustain pressure after the initial sacrifice.
lessons.alternativeNote: The supplied ...Bg3 saves the h2 bishop, but White has Bxh7+ in that branch. The move ...h5 prioritizes the pawn break instead. Compare the resulting checks and rook access rather than assuming that preserving the attacked bishop must be Black's first priority.

review.notes: Independently reviewed all 31 new lessons against the exact before/after FENs, ordered context, and supplied candidate continuations. Preserved all stable keys and excluded the nine existingAccepted lessons. Corrected the implication that Re1 alone releases the f3 knight from defending e5, added the concrete f2 defense created by castling, and clarified how exchanges free the knight. Sharpened the connected-pawn explanation, the protected bishop check and checking fork, the queen routes opened and blocked by pawn moves, and the distinct direct-pawn and discovered-rook checks. White's later moves are presented as defensive resistance rather than automatic improvements or a refutation of Black's sacrifice. Bounded and varying candidate evaluations are not treated as proof of forced play or mate. All required fields and length ranges reviewed.
